title: The First Warning
excerpt: Maya escapes a seemingly impossible accident and finds a photograph of herself taken inside her locked apartment.
content:
Day Two — 12:03 a.m.

Maya stood in the middle of her living room, unable to move.

Her mother was outside.

Eleven years of unanswered questions, eleven years of birthdays without phone calls, eleven years of searching through old photographs and missing-person reports—and now Evelyn Cole was standing on the other side of her front door.

Alive.

But she had told Maya not to open it.

Behind her mother stood a man in a grey suit. His right hand rested on Evelyn's shoulder, and although Maya couldn't see his expression clearly through the peephole, something about his posture made her skin crawl.

He wasn't helping her mother stand.

He was holding her in place.

Maya reached for the door lock.

Then she remembered the message.

The person standing outside your door.

Her fingers froze.

What if the prediction wasn't about the person outside?

What if it was about the person who opened the door?

“Maya,” her mother whispered.

The sound was faint, but Maya heard it.

“Please.”

She pressed her palm against the door.

“Mum?”

Evelyn's face crumpled.

“Oh, my baby.”

Maya began to cry.

She had imagined this moment a thousand times. Sometimes, in her imagination, she slapped her mother for leaving. Other times, she held her so tightly that neither of them could breathe. On particularly lonely nights, she imagined her mother explaining everything, telling her that the disappearance had been a mistake and that they could begin again.

She had never imagined fear in her mother's eyes.

“Open the door,” Evelyn pleaded.

The man behind her leaned closer.

Maya could see his reflection in the polished metal of the hallway wall.

He was smiling.

Her phone vibrated.

She looked down.

UNKNOWN NUMBER:

She is lying to you.

Another message appeared.

Ask her what happened at 6:30 p.m.

Maya looked through the peephole again.

Her mother was shaking her head.

“Don't listen to him,” Evelyn whispered.

The man tightened his grip on her shoulder.

“Your daughter has waited eleven years for this moment,” he said calmly. “It would be cruel to disappoint her.”

Maya stepped away from the door.

“Who are you?” she shouted.

The man raised his face toward the peephole.

For the first time, she saw him clearly.

He was perhaps fifty years old, with neatly combed hair, pale eyes, and a thin scar running from his left temple toward his cheekbone.

He looked like someone who belonged in a corporate office, not outside a frightened woman's apartment at midnight.

“My name is Dr. Adrian Shaw,” he replied. “I believe your mother has told you about me.”

“She hasn't told me anything.”

“Then she's been keeping secrets again.”

Evelyn suddenly twisted away from him.

“Run, Maya!”

Shaw grabbed her arm.

A struggle followed.

Maya heard her mother cry out, followed by the sound of something striking the wall.

She reached for the door handle.

Then the lights in the apartment went out.

Darkness swallowed the room.

A second later, someone banged violently against the door.

“Maya, get away from the entrance!” a man's voice shouted.

She recognized the voice.

Daniel.

She had no idea how he had found her, or how he had survived whatever had happened inside the abandoned office building.

But she didn't question it.

She ran toward the bedroom.

Three gunshots rang through the hallway.

A woman screamed.

Then everything went silent.

Maya locked herself inside the bedroom and crouched beside the bed, pressing both hands over her mouth.

For several minutes, she heard nothing except her own breathing.

Then her phone vibrated.

A message appeared.

You made the right choice.

Maya stared at it in disbelief.

Another message followed.

Unfortunately, someone else paid the price.

Her phone began ringing.

Daniel.

She answered immediately.

“Where are you?”

“Inside your building,” he whispered. “Don't come out yet.”

“Where's my mother?”

Silence.

“Daniel, where is she?”

“I don't know.”

“Did you see her?”

“Yes.”

“Was that really her?”

“I believe so.”

Maya squeezed her eyes shut.

“What happened outside my door?”

“I heard the gunshots. By the time I reached the hallway, the man was gone.”

“And my mother?”

Daniel hesitated.

“She was gone too.”

Maya lowered the phone.

“No.”

“Maya, listen to me. I've called someone I trust. We're going to find her.”

“No!” Her voice broke. “You don't understand. She's been gone for eleven years. I just saw her. I heard her voice. I can't lose her again.”

“You haven't lost her.”

“How can you know that?”

“Because she left something for you.”

Maya went silent.

Daniel continued.

“When I reached your door, there was an envelope on the floor. I've got it with me.”

“What's inside?”

“I haven't opened it.”

“Bring it upstairs.”

“I can't.”

“Why not?”

“Because there's someone standing at the entrance to your building.”

Maya felt a chill move through her body.

“Who?”

“I don't know. He's been watching the stairs for ten minutes.”

She looked toward the bedroom window.

Her apartment was on the fourth floor. Beyond the glass, the city stretched into the distance, its lights scattered across the wet streets.

A dark shape stood on the rooftop of the building opposite hers.

Someone was watching her.

Daniel whispered, “Maya, we need to leave.”

Then the call ended.

She waited five minutes before leaving the bedroom.

The living room was dark, but the emergency light near the kitchen cast a faint glow across the furniture.

Nothing appeared to have been disturbed.

She approached the front door.

A small brown envelope lay on the floor.

Her name was written across it in her mother's handwriting.

Maya picked it up and carried it to the kitchen.

Inside was a photograph and a folded sheet of paper.

The photograph showed Maya as a child, standing beside her mother in front of a hospital building. Her father stood on Evelyn's other side, one hand resting on Maya's shoulder.

She remembered the day.

She had been seven years old.

Her father had told her they were visiting a friend.

But she remembered the building's smell, the bright lights, and the woman who had taken her blood.

She remembered crying.

She remembered her mother arguing with a doctor.

And she remembered her father telling her that everything was going to be fine.

Maya turned the photograph over.

Three words had been written on the back.

PROJECT LAZARUS — SUBJECT 014.

Her hands began to tremble.

She unfolded the paper.

My darling Maya,

If you're reading this, then I've failed to keep you away from them.

I need you to understand something before you begin searching for answers.

Your father was not the man you believed him to be.

Neither was I.

There are things about your childhood that you cannot remember because we made certain you wouldn't.

Do not go to Meridian House.

Do not trust Dr. Shaw.

And above all, do not let anyone take you to the place where you were born.

I love you more than you can imagine.

Mum.

Maya read the letter three times.

Then she sat down.

Her childhood had never been perfect, but she had always believed her parents loved her. Her father had been strict, sometimes distant, but he had worked hard to provide for them. Her mother had been gentle, funny, and endlessly patient.

They had been an ordinary family.

At least, that was what Maya remembered.

Now she wasn't sure she could trust a single memory.

She opened her laptop and searched for Project Lazarus.

Nothing useful appeared.

She tried different spellings, old newspaper archives, medical journals, and government records.

Still nothing.

Finally, she searched the phrase with Meridian House.

One result appeared.

A scanned document from an old medical conference, published online eleven years earlier.

The title read:

Neural Memory Preservation and Post-Traumatic Identity Reconstruction.

The paper had been presented by Dr. Adrian Shaw.

Maya scrolled through the abstract.

It described experimental research into the relationship between traumatic memories, emotional conditioning, and identity formation.

Several pages were missing.

At the bottom of the document was a list of collaborators.

One name stood out.

Dr. Samuel Cole.

Her father.

Maya closed the laptop.

For a long time, she sat motionless at the kitchen table.

Then she remembered something.

Her father had kept a locked drawer in his study. After his death, she had searched the house for important documents but never found the key.

The house had since been sold.

But she still possessed one object from his study.

A small brass key attached to a broken key ring.

She had kept it for years without knowing what it opened.

Maya rushed to her bedroom, pulled open the bottom drawer of her wardrobe, and found the old key inside a jewellery box.

She turned it over in her hand.

On the metal was a tiny engraving.

014.

At that moment, someone knocked on her door.

Maya nearly dropped the key.

“Who is it?”

“It's Daniel.”

She looked through the peephole.

Daniel stood alone in the hallway, his shirt stained with blood near the shoulder.

She unlocked the door.

“What happened to you?”

“Nothing serious.”

“You're bleeding.”

“I've had worse.”

He stepped inside and locked the door behind him.

Maya showed him the photograph and the letter.

He read both in silence.

When he reached the words Project Lazarus, his expression changed.

“You know what this is,” Maya said.

Daniel folded the letter.

“I know what people say about it.”

“Tell me.”

He sat down.

“Before Meridian House closed, there were rumors about a secret research program. Officially, it was a medical project studying trauma and memory. Unofficially, people believed the researchers were testing ways to manipulate what people remembered.”

“Manipulate memories?”

“Not like erasing an entire life. More like altering how someone experiences a traumatic event, or making certain memories difficult to access.”

Maya looked at the childhood photograph.

“Could they have done that to me?”

Daniel didn't answer immediately.

“It's possible that someone tried to influence what you remembered. But this photograph alone doesn't prove anything.”

“My father was involved.”

“Yes.”

“And my mother says they made sure I wouldn't remember something.”

“I know.”

Maya stared at him.

“How do you know?”

Daniel looked away.

The silence that followed was more revealing than any answer.

“You knew about this before tonight,” she whispered.

“Maya—”

“How long have you known?”

He rubbed his face.

“Since your father died.”

She stood up so quickly that the chair scraped against the floor.

“You've known for years?”

“I discovered a file among your father's documents. I didn't understand everything in it, but I recognized the Meridian House connection.”

“And you said nothing?”

“I was trying to protect you.”

“Everyone keeps saying that!”

Her voice echoed through the apartment.

“My mother disappeared to protect me. My father hid the truth to protect me. You lied to protect me. And now somebody is killing people while telling me I have seven days to live.”

She pointed at the door.

“Get out.”

Daniel remained seated.

“Before I leave, there's something else you need to see.”

He reached into his jacket and removed a small memory card.

“I found this in the abandoned office building. It was hidden behind the photograph of your mother.”

Maya took it.

“What is it?”

“A video file. The footage is dated eleven years ago.”

She inserted the card into her laptop.

The video opened.

At first, the screen showed only a corridor.

A hospital corridor.

A young girl sat in a chair beside a closed door. Her legs swung back and forth, and she held a stuffed rabbit against her chest.

Maya leaned closer.

The girl was her.

She looked about seven years old.

A man entered the frame.

Her father.

He crouched in front of the little girl and spoke to her.

Although the audio was poor, Maya could make out several words.

“Do you remember what we discussed?”

The child shook her head.

Her father smiled sadly.

“Good. That's good.”

He took the stuffed rabbit from her and placed it on the chair beside her.

Then he looked directly toward the camera.

“Begin the procedure.”

The screen went black.

Maya couldn't breathe.

“What procedure?” she whispered.

Daniel looked as if he wanted to disappear.

“I don't know.”

She played the video again.

This time, she noticed a detail she had missed.

A reflection in the glass door behind her father.

A woman standing inside the room.

Her mother.

Evelyn was crying.

She was holding a document.

And on that document was Maya's photograph.

Underneath it were the words:

SUBJECT 014 — MEMORY SUPPRESSION APPROVED.

Maya closed the laptop.

“No,” she whispered.

Daniel moved toward her.

She stepped away.

“Don't touch me.”

He stopped.

For several minutes, neither of them spoke.

Then Maya's phone rang.

Unknown number.

She answered without thinking.

A familiar voice spoke.

“Have you found the key?”

Maya looked down at the brass key in her palm.

“Who are you?”

“You're asking the wrong question again.”

“Are you the person sending the countdown messages?”

“Yes.”

“Why are you doing this?”

“Because your father made a mistake.”

“What mistake?”

“He allowed you to live.”

Maya felt a wave of nausea.

“You're going to kill me?”

“No.”

The answer was so unexpected that she almost laughed.

“Then why tell me I have seven days left?”

“Because seven days is all you have before they find what you're looking for.”

“What am I looking for?”

The man paused.

Then he said, “The truth about the woman you killed.”

Maya's heart stopped.

“I've never killed anyone.”

“That's what you remember.”

She gripped the phone.

“Who was she?”

“Her name was Rebecca.”

Maya had never heard that name before.

The man continued.

“She was twenty-three years old. She had a little brother. She worked at Meridian House, and she discovered what your father was doing.”

Maya felt the room spinning around her.

“What happened to her?”

“She disappeared.”

“Like my mother?”

“No.”

The man's voice hardened.

“Unlike your mother, Rebecca never came back.”

The call ended.

Maya stared at the screen.

Daniel looked at her.

“What did he say?”

She told him everything.

When she mentioned Rebecca's name, Daniel's face drained of color.

“You know her,” Maya said.

He didn't deny it.

“Daniel?”

He walked to the window and stared into the darkness.

“Rebecca was my sister.”

Maya felt as if the floor had disappeared beneath her.

“Your sister?”

“She worked at Meridian House. She was a medical records assistant. Eleven years ago, she discovered that patient files were being altered.”

“And you never told me?”

“I didn't know you were connected to it until I found your father's documents.”

“What happened to her?”

Daniel closed his eyes.

“I spent years looking for her. I found evidence that she had been taken to a private facility after the fire. Every record after that disappeared.”

“Did she die?”

“I don't know.”

Maya sat down.

For the first time, she understood why Daniel had stayed close to her investigation, why he had continued helping her even when the story threatened his career.

He wasn't simply protecting her.

He was searching for his sister.

And someone had just told Maya that she was responsible for Rebecca's death.

At 5:12 p.m., Daniel left to meet his contact at the police department.

Maya stayed home, reviewing every file she had collected about Meridian House.

At 5:47 p.m., she found a document hidden inside the scanned medical conference paper.

It was a list of patients admitted to Meridian House during the final year of its operation.

Most names had been redacted.

But one entry remained visible.

REBECCA OKAFOR — ADMISSION DATE: 14 OCTOBER 2015.

The next line was almost entirely blacked out.

Only two words remained.

TRANSFERRED: SUBJECT 014.

Maya stared at the screen.

Subject 014.

Her.

She checked the date.

October 14, 2015.

The same week her mother disappeared.

The same month the research wing burned.

And the same period in which Maya's childhood memories began to blur.

She searched her personal files for the number.

Then she found an old photograph of her seventh birthday.

Her father stood beside a birthday cake, smiling at the camera.

Her mother was behind him.

And beside her mother stood a young woman Maya didn't recognize.

A woman with dark hair and a small scar across her chin.

Maya enlarged the photograph.

On the back, someone had written a name.

Rebecca.

She was standing in the family home.

She was holding Maya's hand.

And she was wearing the same silver pendant that Maya had seen in the footage of the shooting that morning.

Maya's phone vibrated.

A message appeared.

Day Two is almost over.

Another followed.

Tomorrow, you will discover why your father chose you.

Then a third.

At 6:30 p.m., someone you love will die.

Maya looked at the clock.

6:12 p.m.

She called Daniel.

No answer.

She tried again.

Straight to voicemail.

At 6:18 p.m., a message arrived from his number.

Don't come looking for me.

Maya stood up.

Something was wrong.

Daniel would never send a message like that without explaining why.

She called the police officer he had mentioned earlier, but the number was switched off.

Then she opened the location-sharing application they had used during previous investigations.

Daniel's phone was moving.

Its location showed a building on the outskirts of Lagos.

Meridian House.

Maya grabbed her keys and ran outside.

She didn't think about the countdown, the threats, or the possibility that she was walking into a trap.

She thought only about Daniel.

At 6:27 p.m., she reached the abandoned facility.

The main gate stood open.

Inside, the building was dark.

She parked near the entrance and hurried through the lobby.

“Daniel!”

Her voice echoed through the empty corridors.

She followed the sound of a phone ringing toward the old research wing.

The door was locked.

A keypad glowed beside it.

Maya tried the brass key.

Nothing happened.

Then she remembered the engraving.

014.

She entered the numbers.

The lock clicked.

The door opened.

Inside, a single fluorescent light illuminated a hospital bed.

Daniel lay on it, his hands tied to the metal frame.

His face was bruised.

A man stood beside him, wearing a white medical coat.

Maya recognized him immediately.

Dr. Adrian Shaw.

“Welcome back, Maya,” he said.

She stepped into the room.

“Let him go.”

Shaw smiled.

“You always were protective of the wrong people.”

He lifted a remote control.

A monitor beside the bed switched on.

The screen showed a live video feed of Daniel's apartment.

A woman stood in the living room, holding a gun.

Maya recognized her.

Rebecca.

Daniel's sister.

Shaw watched Maya's expression.

“Your editor has spent eleven years trying to find her. Your mother has spent eleven years trying to hide her. And your father spent his final years trying to make sure you never remembered her.”

Maya stared at the screen.

Rebecca raised her head.

For one brief moment, she looked directly into the camera.

Then she spoke.

“I'm sorry, Maya.”

The video cut out.

Shaw turned toward the bed.

“It's 6:29.”

Maya looked at the clock on the wall.

One minute remained.

“What's going to happen?” she demanded.

Shaw placed the remote on the bedside table.

“You've been told someone you love will die at 6:30.”

He looked at Daniel.

“Perhaps you should ask yourself why the prediction has always been so accurate.”

The clock changed.

6:30 p.m.

A sharp electronic tone sounded from the monitor.

Daniel stopped moving.

Maya rushed to his side.

“Daniel?”

No response.

She shook his shoulder.

“Daniel, wake up!”

His body remained still.

Shaw watched without emotion.

Maya pressed her fingers against Daniel's neck.

Nothing.

“No,” she whispered.

She began chest compressions, desperately trying to remember the first-aid instructions she had once learned.

“Come on, Daniel. Please.”

She counted aloud.

One.

Two.

Three.

She kept going until her arms hurt.

Then Daniel suddenly gasped.

Maya stumbled backward.

He coughed violently, his eyes opening.

A thin tube had been hidden beneath his collar. Shaw had used a medical device to suppress Daniel's breathing and pulse temporarily, creating the appearance of death.

Maya turned toward the doctor.

“You sick bastard!”

Shaw calmly adjusted his coat.

“You see? The prediction was correct. Someone you love died at 6:30.”

“He wasn't dead!”

“According to the equipment, he was.”

Maya stared at him in horror.

“You manipulated the prediction.”

“No, Maya. I manipulated your understanding of it.”

Shaw approached her.

“That's what your father did, too.”

He reached into his pocket and removed a photograph.

It showed a little girl standing beside a hospital bed.

Maya recognized the girl immediately.

It was her.

The woman in the bed was Rebecca.

Shaw placed the photograph in her hand.

“Now you understand why you were chosen.”

Maya looked down.

On the back of the photograph were four words.

YOU WERE THE FIRST.

The lights went out.

When they came back on, Shaw was gone.

The door stood open.

Daniel was sitting up on the bed, breathing heavily.

Maya turned toward him.

“What does he mean?”

Daniel stared at the photograph.

Then he looked at her with an expression she had never seen before.

Fear.

“Maya,” he whispered, “I think your father made you the first successful subject of Project Lazarus.”

Her phone vibrated.

A new message appeared.

Five days left.

Then another.

Tomorrow, you will remember Rebecca.

Maya looked at the photograph again.

The woman in the hospital bed had her eyes open.

She was staring directly at the camera.

And beneath the bed, barely visible in the darkness, was a second figure.

A little girl.

Holding a bloodstained knife.

Maya dropped the photograph.

Because the little girl was her.

END OF EPISODE 2

Next: Episode 3 — The Dead Woman.
